articles.title: Striking Photos Reveal the Legacy of Yellowstone’s Wolves—30 Years After Their Return
articles.summary: Three decades after the animals were reintroduced to the national park, revisit the legendary predators through National Geographic's archives.
articles.body:
A yearling wolf from Yellowstone National Park's Druid Peak pack in May 2008. Formed in 1996 from wolves brought from Canada, the pack became one of Yellowstone's most famous, dominating the Lamar Valley and engaging in fierce rivalries with neighboring packs. At its peak in 2001, it numbered 37 wolves—the largest pack ever recorded in the park. Tom Murphy, National Geographic Image Collection

Once eradicated by the government in the 1920s to protect livestock, gray wolves made a historic comeback in 1995 and 1996. In the three decades since, they've become some of North America's most iconic—and controversial—wild animals.

Some have become legends in their own right. There's Wolf 8, a runt that eventually rose to leader status, and O-6, a formidable hunter known for taking down elk single-handedly. O-6 and her daughter, Spitfire, were both killed legally by hunters after wandering beyond the park's borders.

Whole packs have also become household names. For instance, Mollie's Pack, originally known as the Crystal Creek Pack, descends from the first animals reintroduced to the park from Canada. The park's oldest pack, it's known for hunting bison many times the wolves' size.

Of course, gray wolves have also sparked controversy. The animals have been protected, legislated, appealed, delisted , and re-listed more times than most people can keep track of. While hunting is prohibited within Yellowstone, wolves that cross the park's boundaries can be legally hunted under state regulations.

Few people have witnessed the wolves' return and evolution as closely as Rick McIntyre, who has spent more than three decades observing them in Yellowstone.

"It was May of 1995, and I'd just been hired by the National Park Service to explain the reintroduction plan to the public," says McIntyre, author of nearly a dozen books about the park's wolves, including his most recent biography, My Life With Wolves: How I Became the Storyteller for the Yellowstone Packs . "I remember thinking that my goal for that summer was to just see one of the newly reintroduced wolves, and if I did that, I'd be the happiest guy in the world."

Instead, McIntyre found himself observing the animals nearly every day. "None of us, and certainly not me, was prepared for that visibility," he says. "It was a very magical time in the history of Yellowstone."

Most mornings, McIntyre was among the first to arrive in the park's Lamar Valley, setting up his spotting scope to observe the wolves as the sun rose and the mists lifted. Before long, park visitors would be lined up behind him, eager to see the charismatic mammals through his lens.

"Decades later, I'm still doing that," he laughs. "I had my 10,000th day a few years ago."

Over those thousands of days, McIntyre has watched wolves rise and fall in rank and entire packs form and dissolve. "Like human empires, wolf packs tend not to last forever," he says.

Decades of observation have also changed how researchers understand wolf behavior. Although researchers once thought males dominated pack decisions, McIntyre says females often play a leading role.

"When you really watch them over a long time, it's clear that it's the alpha female making all the decisions," he says. "She decides who to mate with, and where they are going to den, and how to deal with enemy packs. She's definitely in charge."

Our understanding of the wolves' impact on Yellowstone's ecosystem has also changed.

For years, their return has been credited with triggering a trophic cascade—a chain reaction in which changes to one species affect others throughout an ecosystem. By preying on elk, which had grown in number and heavily browsed aspen and willow trees, wolves helped those plants recover, setting off changes that benefited other species throughout the ecosystem.

But just how much of that recovery can be attributed to wolves remains a subject of scientific debate.

"The elimination of the wolves back in 1926, and then the subsequent reintroduction of wolves in 1995 and 1996—those events, did not occur in isolation," says Dan Macnulty , an ecologist at Utah State University.

Macnulty has been studying the broader environmental changes that have shaped Yellowstone over the past century. He argues that the popular account of the wolves' return overlooks the many other factors that have influenced the park's ecosystem.

Around the time wolves were eradicated, mountain lions were also heavily hunted. Park managers provided hay to supplement Yellowstone's dwindling bison population, which also benefited elk. Parts of Lamar Valley were plowed and planted, while vegetation along waterways, including willows, was deliberately burned.

"The point of me saying all of this to you is that our expectation that wolf reintroduction in the 1990s would somehow reverse all of that massive damage is totally unrealistic," says Macnulty.

That doesn't mean wolves haven't affected Yellowstone's elk, aspen, or other species. Rather, Macnulty's research suggests that their influence on the broader ecosystem is likely much less powerful than originally estimated .

Other researchers disagree. In a 2026 response to Macnulty's findings , scientists argued that the recovery of Yellowstone's aspen trees remains strong and ecologically significant, even if it hasn't occurred uniformly across the landscape.

But he says judging the success of the wolves' return by how much they transformed the landscape misses the point. Restoring the ecosystem was never the original goal.

"When I was assisting with the reintroduction back in the 1990s as a technician on the Wolf Project, nobody had really heard of a trophic cascade. And it certainly hadn't been used to propose why wolves should be reintroduced to Yellowstone," says Macnulty. "We were doing it simply because it was the right thing to do, from the conservation standpoint."

Today, Yellowstone's wolves remain both a powerful tourist draw as well as a topic of intense scrutiny. As researchers continue to uncover how the predators interact with the park's ever-changing ecosystem, Macnulty believes their story offers a broader lesson.

"We have to be more cautious and more humble in our power to understand how these systems work, and just appreciate all the species that are there for their own sake," says Macnulty.

Jason Bittel is a National Geographic Explorer and author of Grizzled: Love Letters to 50 of North America's Least Understood Animals, now available from National Geographic Books.

articles.title: Space won't wait for those who fall behind
articles.summary: Space is back in the language of national ambition.
articles.body: Space is back in the language of national ambition. On Nov 3, the day Americans went to the polls for the midterm elections, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation titled “The American Declaration of Freedom in Space”. It speaks of returning Americans to the Moon by 2028, establishing a permanent lunar presence and eventually sending an American to Mars. It also makes an unmistakable claim: the nation that leads in space will shape humanity’s future.The document does not create a new legal order or confer sovereignty over celestial bodies. But it does put the scale of American ambition on record.[Also read: TOI NEWS REPORT FROM LAST WEEK]Isro has earned a reputation for launching satellites for domestic and international customers and undertaking complex missions. But its 2026 launch record is a reminder of how much rests on reliable access to orbit.As of Nov 7, it has made three orbital launch attempts: two successes and one failure. GSLV-F17 placed EOS-05 in its intended orbit in Sept; GSLV-F18 launched the NVS-03 on Oct 30. PSLV-C62 encountered an anomaly towards the end of its third stage in Jan and failed to place its payloads in their intended orbits.Three launches are too small a sample to judge Isro’s overall reliability, and one failure cannot erase decades of achievement. But the record raises a larger question: can India build the launch capacity, cadence and resilience its ambitions require? A space programme cannot plan around occasional successes. It needs to launch when required, at a sustainable cost, and at a frequency that serves scientific, strategic and commercial needs.This is not a new argument. I have written before about investing in launch vehicles and why countries sometimes need capabilities they could buy elsewhere. The fundamentals have not changed; the urgency has. Recent developments underline that space is moving beyond access as an occasional achievement towards access as an industrial capability.The economics are changing too. Reusable launch vehicles, rideshare missions and large satellite constellations have altered expectations about cost, frequency and availability. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development notes that participation in space has widened, but launch activity and supporting infrastructure remain concentrated. In 2025, the US accounted for more than half of global launches, with SpaceX responsible for much of that activity.That concentration matters. A country may own satellites, develop applications and buy launch services, but if it cannot secure access when it needs it, its plans remain exposed to other actors’ capacity, priorities and terms. This is not an argument for making everything at home or shutting out partnerships. It is an argument for ensuring that dependence does not become a strategic vulnerability.India’s launch vehicle portfolio must evolve. PSLV has served the country well, LVM-3 provides heavier lift capability, and SSLV is intended for the small-satellite market. But having a rocket for every payload class is not enough. These systems must be dependable, competitive and available at a frequency customers can plan around. Reusability can reduce costs, but requires sustained work on propulsion, materials, guidance, recovery and operations.Isro cannot do all this alone. India’s private space sector must supplement the agency, not be cast as its rival or treated merely as a contractor waiting for work. Isro has built the foundations; private companies can add scale, capital, specialised products, manufacturing capacity and commercial agility. They can develop launch vehicles, satellites, components and data services, while Isro advances research, strategic missions and technologies that can later move into wider use.There are encouraging signs. The govt counted more than $618 million in private investment by March 31, and 113 authorisations to non-govt entities by mid-year — consultancy firms put the investment numbers much higher. In July, Skyroot’s Vikram-1 became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit from Indian soil. The reforms that opened the sector in 2020 are beginning to produce capabilities beyond the public programme.But an ecosystem is measured by more than the number of start-ups, funding announcements or authorisations. It must deliver reliable products, win customers, retain talent, build intellectual property and develop businesses that can survive beyond a single contract or funding round.It also needs trust. Some of the developments of the past few days, including two companies choosing to air their differences in public, have been unpalatable. I do not intend to name those involved or revisit the exchanges; this column should not give the episode more oxygen.Competition is necessary, sometimes fierce. But a young sector seeking credibility must also show professional maturity. Public disputes that distract from the work risk weakening confidence in the very ecosystem everyone says they want to build.The private sector also needs a predictable regulator, access to facilities, patient capital and a domestic customer base willing to procure innovative products. Equally, companies must understand that public investment and policy support are not entitlements. They have to earn confidence through performance, transparency and the ability to deliver. A strong Isro is necessary, but a strong Isro alone will not be sufficient.India does not have to imitate the American model or match every ambition in Trump’s proclamation. Nor does it need to pursue self-sufficiency in every component. It does need to decide what capabilities are too important to leave entirely to others.The test of space power is not simply whether a country can place a satellite in orbit, or announce a mission to the Moon. It is whether it can keep going back, carry out increasingly complex work, develop technologies of its own and sustain an industry around those capabilities.The next space race may not be won by the country that makes the grandest declaration. It may be won by the one that can launch reliably, frequently and affordably, while building an ecosystem capable of turning access to space into lasting national capability. For India, the task is not just to reach space. It is to remain in the race on its own terms.Postscript:The Parallax here is that reaching space and having the power to shape what happens there are two different things. A rocket can take a country into orbit. Only a sustained national capability can keep it there, on its own terms.

articles.title: MICHAEL GUILLEN: Science's fantastic discoveries are making religion more credible
articles.summary: Dark matter and dark energy account for 95% of the cosmos, meaning science is based on only 5% of what's real, deepening the universe's mystery.
articles.body: I’ll never forget the time I received my very own microscope for Christmas; suddenly, a drop of pond water became a teeming cosmos of strange, wriggling creatures. Nor will I ever forget peering through my first telescope; suddenly, the moon’s eerie, cratered surface exploded to life and looked close enough for me to touch. Those two boyhood experiences tell the entire, exciting, unexpected story of science in a nutshell. With every new, more powerful imaging device, scientists have gradually, spectacularly brought to light the once-shrouded secrets of the microscopic and macroscopic cosmos. Throughout this long, impressive eye-opening drama, scientists have justifiably boasted about how their discoveries are systematically ridding our species of its hoary, benighted superstitions, religion included. This conceit is displayed in the title of Carl Sagan’s book "The Demon-Haunted World: Science As a Candle in the Dark." For Carl — a professor of mine at Cornell — science was indeed the great, bright hope for a terribly dim-witted world. NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN But, the story of science hasn’t turned out as the optimists prophesied, not by a long shot. That’s because modern science is discovering there’s far, far more to reality than meets the eye, than even our most sensitive instruments can see. That we live in a demon-haunted cosmos after all — one infested with invisible, inscrutable spirits with such names as dark matter and dark energy. As a grad student at Cornell, I recall learning about what my astronomy professors called the "missing mass problem," a mystery dating back to 1933, when Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky used data from Mount Wilson Observatory’s powerful Hooker telescope to study clusters of galaxies. To his astonishment, Zwicky discovered that galaxies are swarming within each cluster like bees in a hive at a much faster clip than conventional physics can explain. NEIL DEGRASSE TYSON DARES GOVERNMENT TO 'JUST SHOW THE ALIEN,' AS DISCLOSURE FERVOR CONTINUES TO GROW In class, I learned that these clustered galaxies would need to have roughly 10 times more mass to explain their unusual swiftness. This means that most of the galaxies’ collective mass is "missing" — is invisible to us. Zwicky called this ghostly mass "dunkle materie," German for dark matter. Scientists today offer many fanciful, high-brow explanations for dark matter, but the plain truth is that, nearly a century after Zwicky’s discovery, we still have no idea whatsoever what it is. For now, the consensus is that, like conventional matter, dunkle materie is gravitational in nature — which is why it can tug on and speed up the clustered galaxies. But, very unlike conventional matter, dunkle materie does not radiate or reflect light — which is why it’s invisible. FROM COCKROACH MILK TO STEPPING ON SNAKES, IG NOBEL AWARDS CELEBRATES SCIENCE AT ITS ODDEST It wasn’t the first time data from the powerful Hooker telescope near Pasadena, California, delivered a scientific bombshell. Back in 1929, American lawyer-turned-astronomer Edwin Hubble used that very same instrument to discover that the universe is expanding. Thereafter, astronomers simply assumed the expansion was slowing down, owing to the universe’s collective gravity putting the brakes on it. But, in 1998, the story of science took yet another startling turn to the dark side, when two separate teams of astronomers discovered that the expansion of our universe is actually speeding up, not slowing down. This implies the existence of an invisible, inscrutable, repulsive "something" that permeates the whole of our universe. At a 1998 symposium at the Australian Academy of Science in Canberra, University of Chicago cosmologist Michael Turner gave the "something" a name: dark energy. But giving the phantom material a name doesn’t explain it. To this day, as with dark matter, dark energy remains a complete mystery — notwithstanding the countless published but unsupported attempts to explain it. The discoveries of dark matter and dark energy would rate little more than a sensational footnote in the impressive story arc of science were it not for one very inconvenient truth. Today, scientists reckon that, all told, the two shadowy spirits account for 95% of the observable cosmos (never mind the existence of the totally unobservable cosmos beyond the Cosmic Horizon). Ninety-five percent! DR MARC SIEGEL: I WENT LOOKING FOR MIRACLES AFTER OCT. 7. I FOUND ANGELS HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT It means that what we see — even with our most powerful, most sophisticated imaging devices — is only 5% of what’s actually "out there." Which means the whole of science — all its experiments, all its theories, the entirety of what it claims to understand about our demon-haunted world — is based on a measly 5% of what’s real. The other 95% of what exists remains a complete mystery. This, in turn, means that, far from demystifying the universe, the twisting, turning story of science is actually mystifying the universe in ways that make religion more credible, not less. The more secrets of the macroscopic and microscopic cosmos science brings to light, the more we discover how very, very, very little we understand about reality. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The more brightly Sagan’s "candle in the dark" burns, the more it reveals the truth of the Apostle Paul’s words, stated nearly 2,000 years ago: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."

articles.title: Birds flap their wings while landing even though it costs energy; a new physics model found a pigeon-sized bird would need more than twice its cruising speed and roughly 60 metres to stop without flapping
articles.summary: In the mobile game Flappy Bird, the bird’s problem is not flying forward, it is staying airborne.
articles.body: In the mobile game Flappy Bird, the bird’s problem is not flying forward, it is staying airborne. Every tap buys a little lift, every pause lets gravity pull it down. Real birds face a harder version of that challenge when they land. They must shed speed, remain controllable, and arrive safely on a branch, ledge, or patch of ground. New physics research, published inProceedings of the Royal Society A, suggests that the wing-flapping birds do during landing is not wasted energy, but a practical solution to a difficult aerodynamic problem.The paradox of landingFlying expenses a lot of energy, and flapping costs more energy than gliding. So it seems logical that a bird approaching a perch should stop flapping, glide in, and touch down as slowly as possible. Yet many birds flap vigorously during the final moments of landing, apparently spending energy at exactly the point where conservation might seem most sensible.Researchers at the University of Manchester Tom Rottier and Ben Parslew, along with Philippe Lavoie of University of Toronto, used mathematical modelling to test whether a bird could achieve a zero-speed landing without powered flapping. Their conclusion: it is theoretically possible, but it demands an approach that is far too fast and long for most real-world landings.For a pigeon-sized bird, the model found that stopping completely without flapping would require an initial speed of more than twice its typical cruising speed, about 60 metres of horizontal travel, and a climb of roughly 20 metres. In practical terms, the bird would need a long runway, a high approach, and considerable speed just to arrive at the perch with no forward motion.Why slowing is hardA bird’s wings generate lift and control through airflow. As the bird slows, the airflow over its wings weakens, and so does its ability to steer, adjust its angle, and recover from disturbances. This creates a fundamental trade-off: a bird wants a low landing speed, but flying too slowly makes precise manoeuvring difficult.Dr Ben Parslew describes landing as more than simply decelerating. A bird must reduce speed while retaining enough aerodynamic authority to complete the manoeuvre safely. The slower it flies, the less control it has; so it must find a way to brake without losing command of its flight.Flapping provides that missing control. By adding bursts of lift and thrust, a bird can adjust its trajectory late in the approach, avoid stalling for too long, and touch down at a manageable speed within a short distance. The energy cost is real, but so is the benefit: a safer, more compact landing.The swoop before the perchThe model also helps explain a familiar sight among birds of prey: the dramatic swoop below a target perch before rising upward to land. Harris’s hawks, for example, have been observed dipping below their landing spot and then gliding up toward it.Earlier work suggested that this manoeuvre minimises the distance travelled after the wings stall, when control is reduced. The new modelling adds an important nuance: the swoop appears to balance two competing goals, arriving at the perch at low speed and limiting the time spent in a stalled, less controllable state.Touchdown speed, the researchers found, has a greater influence on swooping behaviour than previously recognised. In other words, hawks may swoop not merely to shorten the risky post-stall phase, but to manage how fast they arrive at the perch.Landing on the ground is differentPerching birds have one advantage: they can approach from below and rise to their destination, converting speed into height as they close in. A bird landing on the ground cannot do that. It cannot continue below the surface or climb through its landing point.The model showed that a bird making an unpowered ground landing cannot eliminate all of its forward speed before its feet touch down. Some energy inevitably remains, and the bird must absorb it using its wings, legs, or both.That has evolutionary consequences. Stronger legs, muscles, and bones can help a bird withstand the impact of landing, but extra mass makes flight less efficient. The researchers propose that this tension: light enough to fly well, robust enough to land safely, may have helped shape the evolution of birds.From birds to aircraftThe findings could extend beyond ornithology. Understanding how animals manage low-speed control, stall avoidance, and energy absorption may inform the design of drones and other aerial vehicles that must land in confined spaces. Birds solve these problems continuously, without runways, sensors, or fuel calculations.The study’s central insight is counterintuitive but elegant: sometimes the fastest way to slow down is to arrive with enough speed and enough control to manage the final descent.For birds, flapping during landing is not a failure to glide efficiently. It is a calculated investment in safety, precision, and the ability to stop in the small, cluttered spaces where they actually live. In a sense, they are playing a far more sophisticated version of Flappy Bird, one where the goal is not merely to stay aloft, but to arrive exactly where intended, under control.

articles.title: Scientists studied a 444-million-year-old marine fossil that preserved its muscles, tendons and guts but lost its head, legs and outer shell; they named it after the discoverer's mother
articles.summary: A marine creature that lived 444 million years ago has become the subject of a remarkable fossil study after scientists discovered that its internal
articles.body: A marine creature that lived 444 million years ago has become the subject of a remarkable fossil study after scientists discovered that its internal structures survived while much of its outer body disappeared. The fossil, identified as a new species called Keurbos susanae, preserves muscles, tendons, connective structures and digestive remains in exceptional detail, despite lacking its head, legs and most of its hard outer covering. After 25 years of research, University of Leicester palaeontologist Sarah Gabbott formally named the species after her mother, Sue, recognising the encouragement she received to pursue a career in fossil research.The 444-million-year-old fossil preserved its inside organsAccording to the University of Leicester, the fossil presents an unusual reversal of the way many ancient animals are preserved. Most arthropod fossils show their hard external features, including shells and limbs, because these structures generally survive decay more easily than soft tissues. Keurbos susanae instead retains an extraordinary record of its internal anatomy, while much of its external body is missing.The research, published in Papers in Palaeontology on 26 March 2025, describes the species as an exceptionally preserved marine arthropod. In a scientific paper, the internal anatomy of the creature is described as preserved in three dimensions, enabling scientists to view structures seldom observed in fossils from the same period.The fossil's unusual preservation is particularly important because muscles and other soft tissues normally disappear soon after an animal dies. Their survival offers researchers an opportunity to study aspects of ancient animal anatomy that are often absent from the fossil record.What was the creature like when it livedThe scientific paper provides a more detailed picture of the animal's body. Its trunk contained 46 segments arranged in a repeating pattern, gradually becoming narrower towards the rear. The researchers identified structures associated with its internal supporting framework, including connections between body segments and features linked to its muscles.The main specimen measures approximately 43 centimetres in length, making it a substantial animal for the fossil deposit in which it was discovered. Its segmented body and other anatomical characteristics helped researchers identify it as a member of the arthropod group.Arthropods include familiar modern animals such as crabs, lobsters, spiders, insects and millipedes. Their bodies commonly feature repeated sections and a hard external covering. However, the precise evolutionary position of Keurbos susanae remains uncertain because important anatomical features are missing or difficult to interpret.The research notes that the fossil's unusual preservation makes comparisons with other ancient arthropods particularly challenging. Although researchers can confidently recognise it as an arthropod, they cannot establish exactly which evolutionary branch it belongs to.Where was the unique marine fossil discoveredThe specimens came from the Soom Shale, a fossil-rich geological formation in South Africa's Western Cape Province. According to the University of Leicester, the site lies approximately 250 kilometres north of Cape Town, in an area where ancient marine sediments preserve evidence of life from the end of the Ordovician Period.The research paper places the fossils within the Late Ordovician, a period that ended around 444 million years ago. This was a particularly difficult time in Earth's history, when extensive glaciation contributed to one of the planet's major extinction events.The University of Leicester says the marine basin this animal lived in seems to have provided some protection from the worst effects of this environmental upheaval. Researchers found evidence of life in an unusual setting: a community of marine organisms that survived there.The Soom Shale is also known for its distinctive preservation conditions. Its sediments formed in an environment with extremely low oxygen levels and, at times, highly toxic hydrogen sulphide in the water. The scientific paper identifies these conditions as important characteristics of the deposit, although the precise chemical processes responsible for preserving Keurbos susanae remain complex.The fossil lost its outer bodyThe preservation of Keurbos susanae appears to have followed an unusual process that affected its internal and external structures differently.The research paper describes the fossil as displaying a reversed pattern of preservation. Structures that projected beyond the body, including certain specialised plates, retained some details, while much of the external covering and appendages were poorly preserved or missing.Inside the body, however, mineral replacement captured muscles and other delicate anatomical structures in three dimensions. This gave researchers access to details that are rarely available in fossils of ancient arthropods.The authors explain that the fossil's internal supporting structures and muscle anatomy provide a detailed view of the animal's body organisation. Such preservation is rare because these tissues normally decay before they can become part of the fossil record.How did a 25-year study lead to the name SueProfessor Sarah Gabbott, from the University of Leicester's School of Geography, Geology and the Environment, spent 25 years examining the fossil before formally describing the species.The university's announcement explains that Gabbott discovered the material early in her academic career. The fossil proved difficult to interpret, and she continued hoping that additional specimens might reveal more of its anatomy, particularly its head and limbs.The scientific paper ultimately describes two specimens, collected during fieldwork spanning approximately 20 years. However, further discoveries have become increasingly unlikely because quarrying activity has made the principal collecting site difficult to access.Gabbott named the species Keurbos susanae in honour of her mother, Susan Gabbott, affectionately known as Sue. The scientific paper records the name as a tribute to her, while the University of Leicester announcement explains the personal reason behind the decision.Her mother had encouraged her to pursue a career that made her happy, regardless of what that career might be. For Gabbott, that meant studying rocks, discovering fossils and investigating how ancient organisms lived and evolved.The naming also followed a humorous family exchange. According to the university, Sue had recently encouraged her daughter to complete the naming before she herself became fossilised.

articles.title: In a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb, researchers found about 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical traces in human hair, suggesting ritual intoxication among people buried alongside sacrificed horses and other remains
articles.summary: Researchers studying a 2,800-year-old princely tomb in southern Siberia have found about 1,000 cannabis seeds alongside preserved human hair containing
articles.body: Researchers studying a 2,800-year-old princely tomb in southern Siberia have found about 1,000 cannabis seeds alongside preserved human hair containing chemical traces associated with cannabis intoxication. The discovery, reported by Phys.org, ScienceAlert and Discover Magazine, suggests that people buried in the Scythian-era tomb may have used cannabis for its psychoactive effects as part of elaborate funerary rituals involving sacrificed horses and, most likely, human sacrifices.The tomb, known as Tunnug 1, lies in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. An international research team led by archaeologist Gino Caspari of the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology published the findings in the journal Science, describing them as the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of cannabis being used as an intoxicant. Read more details about this discovery, as per the reports, here:A royal tomb in the Valley of the KingsTunnug 1 is a huge burial mound, or kurgan, measuring roughly 140 metres across. It was built in the early eighth century BCE and is associated with the Arzhan culture at the beginning of the Scythian period, a horse-riding society that spread across the Eurasian steppe.The mound concealed elaborate wooden burial chambers, bronze ornaments, beads, weapons and horse-riding equipment. Its scale and complexity indicate that the people buried there were high-ranking members of Scythian society and that those who built the monument commanded substantial resources.The new research focused on six individuals buried in four wooden structures within the mound. In and around those burials, archaeologists recovered more than 1,000 cannabis seeds, many still intact after nearly three millennia.Why the seeds matteredCannabis has long been used for many purposes, including producing oil and fibre, as well as for medicine and intoxication. That makes a cache of seeds difficult to interpret on its own, because it does not automatically prove that people used the plant to alter consciousness.To establish the age of the seeds, the researchers radiocarbon-dated six of them. Those results, combined with other dating evidence, indicate that the cannabis was placed in the grave during the early eighth century BCE.The seeds appear to resemble those of wild cannabis rather than modern domesticated varieties. Cannabis grows naturally across temperate Central Asia, so the plants may have been gathered locally rather than cultivated specifically for psychoactive properties.Chemical evidence in human hairThe decisive evidence came from preserved human hair found in the central burial chamber. Hair can retain molecular traces of substances that circulated through the body while a person was alive, because those compounds become trapped in the keratin structure as hair grows.Using methods including high-resolution mass spectrometry, the researchers analysed several hair samples. They found clear signals consistent with cannabinol, or CBN, a compound that forms when tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, oxidises over time. They also detected weaker signals whose molecular mass was consistent with THC itself.According to Caspari, the combination of cannabis seeds and molecular traces in hair from the same grave suggests that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties. The study therefore links the plant remains directly to evidence of consumption, rather than relying on seeds alone.What researchers still cannot proveThe findings are significant, but they leave important questions unanswered. The researchers cannot reliably determine how much cannabis was consumed, how potent the ancient plants were, or whether the active compounds entered the body through inhalation or ingestion.It is also not possible to say from the evidence whether the cannabis was deliberately cultivated for higher THC content. The seeds likely came from wild plants, and the study does not establish a specific method of consumption.Later archaeological sites in Central Asia have produced cannabinoid residues in vessels and on heated stones, which more clearly point to inhalation. At Tunnug 1, however, the evidence shows exposure to psychoactive cannabis, not the exact way it was used.Cannabis within a sacrificial ritualThe burial context gives the discovery a striking dimension. The researchers say the tomb contained extensive horse sacrifices, and they believe human sacrifices were likely as well. Earlier work at the site identified the remains of 18 horses arranged on the burial mound, and further excavation has revealed dozens more horse sacrifices along with scattered human bones.Many of the horses were placed with human bones in arrangements that evoke ancient accounts of spectral riders guarding Scythian rulers. The researchers suggest that cannabis may have played a role in calming individuals who were to be included in these rituals, although that interpretation remains a possibility rather than a proven conclusion.The presence of seeds in an elaborate burial also suggests that cannabis held cultural importance. Seeds are not ordinarily included in high-status graves unless they carried symbolic, practical or ritual meaning for the people conducting the ceremony.What comes nextThe team has begun sequencing DNA from the ancient plant remains. Because DNA preservation at the site is excellent, the researchers hope to learn more about whether the cannabis was cultivated and how the plant spread across the ancient world.For now, the study reframes early cannabis use as more than a pharmacological curiosity. The researchers argue that it shows how ancient societies experimented with and ritualised the psychoactive qualities of the botanical world.The discovery at Tunnug 1 does not prove that cannabis was central to every Scythian burial, nor does it reveal the full meaning of the ceremonies held there. But it provides the earliest securely dated direct evidence that people used cannabis for intoxication, and it places that use within one of the most dramatic funerary settings yet studied from the early Scythian world.

articles.title: First foreign astronaut on China’s Tiangong station will be from Pak
articles.summary: BENGALURU: China has confirmed that a Pakistani astronaut will become the first foreign national to board its Tiangong space station, joining the
articles.body: BENGALURU: China has confirmed that a Pakistani astronaut will become the first foreign national to board its Tiangong space station, joining the Shenzhou-24 crewed mission as a payload specialist.The astronaut will be selected from two Pakistani candidates, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, who have undergone months of training in China. The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), which announced the decision on Nov 7, has not named the candidate or specified a launch date.The mission will mark the first joint crewed flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China’s human spaceflight programme. TOI has been tracking the developments for several weeks. Both the Chinese and Pakistani agencies did not respond to multiple queries sent since late Sept.As per official Chinese media, after a short stay aboard Tiangong, the Pakistani astronaut will return to Earth aboard Shenzhou-23, which docked with the station in May 2026.The agreement between China and Pakistan was signed in Feb 2025, covering astronaut selection, training and participation in Chinese space-station missions. Following a three-stage assessment, Ali and Daud were shortlisted and sent to China for training alongside Chinese counterparts. One will fly while the other remains a backup.For Pakistan, the mission represents its entry into human spaceflight. For China, it is an opportunity to demonstrate that Tiangong can serve as an international platform for crewed missions as the International Space Station (ISS) approaches retirement.China completed its space station in 2022, having developed an independent human spaceflight programme after being excluded from the ISS partnership. Now, Beijing is looking to extend Tiangong's reach through international partnerships.The Pakistan mission is an early demonstration of that approach. China has also been working with other countries on space exploration, including lunar missions, and offering opportunities for international participation.The timing matters. The ISS, the world’s only mature, multilateral space station, is approaching the end of its operational life. Tiangong could increasingly become an alternative for countries seeking access to human spaceflight, scientific experiments and operational experience in orbit.The emerging competition, therefore, is not simply about who can build a station or send astronauts into space. It is also about who can attract partners and shape the frameworks for future exploration.For India, the development adds a geopolitical dimension to its human spaceflight ambitions. Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla’s Axiom-4 mission to the ISS last year gave India its first human spaceflight experience since Rakesh Sharma (1984). But its next steps remain centred on indigenous capability through Gaganyaan, followed by the Bhartiya Antriksh Station (BAS), and a crewed Moon landing.India signed the US-led Artemis Accords in June 2023, while China and Russia are pursuing the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) framework. These competing initiatives could influence technological standards, resource-use principles and the governance of activities beyond Earth.India’s challenge is to work with different space powers without becoming confined to their geopolitical choices. The Pakistani mission also raises a question for New Delhi: whether building indigenous infrastructure alone will be sufficient, or whether India must simultaneously seek greater access to international experience and partnerships.A few days aboard Tiangong will not give Pakistan an independent human spaceflight capability. But it will give the country a place in China’s crewed space programme and Beijing another partner as it expands its international ambitions.For India, the message is not that it must follow Pakistan’s route or choose between Washington and Beijing. The next space race will be shaped as much by partnerships and influence as by rockets and spacecraft. India’s ability to safeguard its strategic autonomy will depend on ensuring it has a voice in shaping that future.

articles.title: Study finds forgotten Cold War nuclear base in Greenland was once ice-free, with summers 4.7°C warmer about 416,000 years ago
articles.summary: A forgotten Cold War military base buried beneath Greenland's ice is giving scientists an unusual glimpse into a much warmer Earth.
articles.body: A forgotten Cold War military base buried beneath Greenland's ice is giving scientists an unusual glimpse into a much warmer Earth. Researchers examined sediment recovered from Camp Century in northwestern Greenland, a site built by the US Army Corps of Engineers in 1959 and abandoned in 1967. The sediment contained biological markers that allowed scientists to reconstruct summer temperatures and moisture conditions about 416,000 years ago, during Marine Isotope Stage 11. They found that summers were about 4.7°C warmer than modern conditions, while the site was ice-free despite now sitting beneath 1,387 metres of ice. The findings offer new clues about Greenland's sensitivity to prolonged warmth.Camp Century was built during the Cold War beneath Greenland's iceCamp Century was constructed by the US Army Corps of Engineers in 1959 beneath the surface of the Greenland Ice Sheet. The facility was part military experiment and part research station, with the US Army investigating whether infrastructure and ballistic missiles could operate beneath the ice. A portable nuclear generator powered the base, which housed between 85 and 200 soldiers. The larger Project Iceworm plan was ultimately rejected, and year-round operations ended in 1964. Seasonal operations continued until the facility was abandoned in 1967, leaving the base buried beneath accumulating snow and ice.Sediment beneath the ice preserved evidence of a warmer GreenlandThe new study, ‘Holocene-like summer climate during Marine Isotope Stage 11 in northwestern Greenland’, published in Climate of the Past, focuses on a 3.44-metre sediment core recovered from beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet at Camp Century. The upper sediment units were dated to about 416,000 ± 38,000 years ago and linked to Marine Isotope Stage 11, an interglacial period when global climate was warmer than during the preceding glacial conditions. Researchers analysed lipid biomarkers, including plant waxes and bacterial compounds known as branched GDGTs. These molecular traces can preserve information about the temperatures and water sources present when the organisms lived, allowing scientists to reconstruct ancient environmental conditions.Scientists found summers were 4.7°C warmer than todayThe biomarkers indicated that the temperature during the months above freezing in northwestern Greenland was 4.7 ± 3.2°C higher than the modern reference period. The researchers said these conditions were similar to or slightly warmer than peak Holocene warmth recorded elsewhere in Greenland. Yet the Camp Century site is now covered by about 1,387 metres of ice. The presence of plant and aquatic biomarkers in the sediments means the landscape around the site must have been ice-free when they were produced. The results therefore provide evidence of a dramatically different landscape beneath an area that is currently buried deep within the ice sheet.Ancient water vapour reveals a greener landscape around the siteThe study also found that summer atmospheric water vapour was about 22 ± 18 per mille enriched in deuterium compared with modern conditions. Researchers interpret this enrichment as evidence that a greater share of the moisture reaching northwestern Greenland came from nearby sources. More ice-free land and vegetation would have increased evapotranspiration, sending locally sourced moisture into the atmosphere. The sediments also contain evidence of aquatic and terrestrial plant life, consistent with an ice-free landscape containing lakes, streams and tundra. The findings suggest that warmer conditions changed not only temperature but also the way moisture moved through the region.The climate was similar to the Holocene but lasted much longerMarine Isotope Stage 11 is particularly useful for understanding Greenland because its temperatures were broadly similar to the Holocene in the North Atlantic region, but the warm interval lasted considerably longer. The researchers found that northwestern Greenland's summer conditions during MIS 11 were broadly comparable to peak Holocene warmth. Despite those similar temperatures, evidence from the study and other records indicates that the Greenland Ice Sheet was more reduced during MIS 11 than during the Holocene. This suggests that the duration of warmth can be crucial to ice-sheet loss, even when temperatures are not exceptionally high.What Greenland’s 416,000-year-old climate record means for the ice sheetThe researchers say the findings have implications beyond reconstructing a distant climate. Greenland's ice sheet contains enough ice to represent about 7.4 metres of potential sea-level rise, making its response to sustained warming an important climate question. The Camp Century evidence suggests that prolonged moderate warmth can contribute to substantial ice-sheet retreat. The authors therefore argue that limiting both the magnitude and duration of summer warming in coming centuries will be important for reducing future ice-sheet loss. A site once created as a Cold War military experiment has consequently become an archive for understanding how Greenland responds when temperatures remain elevated for long periods.

articles.title: Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery. | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mystery solved: Coordinated power drops have been haunting power grid worldwide, but a team of researchers in Germany found the culprit.
articles.body:
For years, mysterious electrical anomalies have been flummoxing grid managers around the world. Every 60 seconds, the frequency on the grid would drop a tiny bit.

Even weirder: The sags happened at the exact same time on power grids across countries and continents.

It was a mystery that Dirk Witthaut, a researcher at Forschungszentrum Jülich in Germany, couldn’t pass up.

Germany’s largest transmission system operator, Tennet Germany, brought the puzzle to Witthaut, and it took years of investigative and modeling work to determine the cause. From Europe to Australia, the U.S. to Malaysia, the same pattern shows up in the data.

Such frequency drops aren’t unheard of, but they are troubling. And the regularity with which they have been occurring can make the phenomenon feel even more ominous.

The grid’s orderly operation relies on the frequency being kept within a certain range. If the oscillations get get too large, or if grid operators don’t know the cause and respond improperly, they can lead to blackouts. Even if the sags don’t cause blackouts, they can damage equipment in power plants if they go unchecked, especially in hydropower turbines.

Hydropower plants have historically been a main driver of so-called ultra-low frequency oscillations (UFLOs). Every turbine vibrates, and if those vibrations occur with a certain regularity, known as the resonant frequency, they can magnify, sometimes to dangerous levels. Think of a wine glass breaking before an opera singer’s mighty pipes — that’s resonance.

So Witthaut and his team started investigating hydropower, the most obvious potential culprit. They used a computer model of a hydropower plant control system on the Scandinavian grid to test the hypothesis.

While they managed to find conditions that could generate a resonance that peaked once per minute, they couldn’t explain why it persisted for so long. Typically, resonances in mechanical systems will come and go, and so will the accompanying signal on the electrical grid. But this frequency drop kept happening minute after minute after minute. Every 60 seconds, without fail.

It then dawned on the team that anything operating with such clockwork required, well, a clock. How else could they explain the uncanny timing?

To that hypothesis, the researchers started close to home, installing more than 80 smart power quality meters around the Jülich campus. The research site is outfitted with medium- and low-voltage distribution lines, transformers, solar panels, and battery energy storage systems that serve as uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). It also has a high-performance computer system as well as the usual office computers powered by much smaller UPS devices. The power quality meters sampled a range of attributes, including frequency, voltage, current, and power, once every three seconds.

Before long, the research team had its answer. The measurements recorded on the transformer attached to the battery energy storage system peaked every minute, just like on the bigger power grids.

It turns out that many stationary batteries, from data center UPSes to large grid-scale batteries , check their state-of-charge every minute. Since these devices are internet-connected, their clocks are in near perfect synchronicity. Every time one checks its charge, the disturbance is imperceptible on the wide grid. But when they all do it together, that disruption becomes apparent.

To find evidence that UPSes were the main culprit on the grid, Witthaut and his team turned to data provided by grid operators. They found their answer in Ireland.

There, data centers have grown to consume a large fraction of the country’s electricity. By 2022, data centers represented 18% of the load on Ireland’s grid, and each facility is served by a fleet of UPSes. Sure enough, between 2016 and 2021, the minute-by-minute frequency drop on the Irish grid quadrupled from 3 milli-Hertz (mHz) in 2016 to 12 mHz in 2021. More recently, some drops have exceeded 20 mHz.

Ireland’s 50 Hz grid is built to withstand swings of plus or minus 200 mHz, though the grid operator would rather limit the swings to 100 mHz. In that range, 20 mHz isn’t a lot, but data centers aren’t the only loads on the grid. If other loads also cause the frequency to sag, the extra bump from every UPS checking its state-of-charge could push the grid toward blackout conditions.

The problem is entirely preventable. Rather than check state-of-charge exactly on the minute, Witthaus and team recommend that UPS and grid-scale battery manufacturers add some randomization to the schedule.

While UPSes are driving the problem today, there’s a risk that the phenomenon could persist. The researchers also tested IoT devices. In devices as diverse as a smart oven and Raspberry Pi clusters, they were able to detect periodic power fluctuations. The fix is also a simple software patch, but many IoT devices go unpatched. A recent study found that less than 3% of IoT devices are running the latest firmware.

Regulators may soon have to step in to demand changes, but they can only address their corner of the grid. Given the global nature of the issue, it’ll ultimately require global coordination. The mystery may be solved, but the problem could remain for years to come.

articles.title: In March 2026, Brazil expanded two Pantanal wildlife reserves by 257,531 acres; Leonardo DiCaprio's conservation group Re:wild says its partners helped support the effort to safeguard jaguar habitat
articles.summary: In the Pantanal, where rivers overflow onto vast floodplains and jaguars wander wetlands and forests, wildlife conservation is increasingly reliant on
articles.body: In the Pantanal, where rivers overflow onto vast floodplains and jaguars wander wetlands and forests, wildlife conservation is increasingly reliant on protecting the landscapes that sustain it. In March 2026, Brazil took a huge step toward that goal by expanding two massive conservation areas by a combined 257,531 acres. The development strengthens protection for one of the world’s most important jaguar habitats while contributing to the protection of threatened species, freshwater ecosystems and communities whose livelihoods depend on the wetlands. Conservation group Re:wild, which was co-founded by actor Leonardo DiCaprio, said it valued the efforts of its partners in the wider push to protect the country’s natural landscapes.Two reserves receive increased protected areaAccording to the Andes Amazon Fund, the expansion took place on March 23, 2026, and includes two federal conservation units in the Brazilian state of Mato Grosso: the Pantanal Mato-Grossense National Park and the Taiamã Ecological Station.The Pantanal Mato-Grossense National Park has been expanded by 116,782 acres, for a total protected area of 450,653 acres. The expansion is especially significant for jaguar conservation as the park is deemed one of the most important jaguar habitats in the world, with an estimated density of around eight jaguars for every 100 square kilometers.The enlarged landscape also protects wildlife like giant otters, maned wolves, giant anteaters and giant armadillos. Its wetlands and lagoons host threatened bird species like the vulnerable cujubi and red-tailed parakeet. Besides reproduction of commercial species like pacu and pintado, the water bodies are also used by artisanal fishing communities across the upper Paraguay River Basin.The second expansion increased the area of the Taiamã Ecological Station by 140,749 acres, to 168,323 acres. The expanded reserve safeguards flooded tropical forests, wetlands and savanna habitats used by jaguars, giant otters, marsh deer, pampas deer and black howler monkeys, the Andes Amazon Fund said.A better network against fires and habitat lossThe expansion is also expected to improve ecological connectivity across the Pantanal beyond simply increasing the size of individual reserves. The larger national park reinforces ties with neighboring protected areas, such as Bolivia’s San Matias Natural Management Area, while Taiamã is better aligned with nearby conservation landscapes, such as the Pantanal Wildlife Reserve.These connections are important because wildlife needs space to move between habitats, especially as seasonal flooding changes the availability of food and shelter. The protected lagoons also help maintain water flows during dry and flooding seasons, supporting fish populations and the larger wetland ecosystem.According to the Andes Amazon Fund, another growing concern is wildfires. The number of fires in the Pantanal in 2024 rose as much as 529% over the historical average. Expanding protected areas can help to strengthen landscape-level conservation and reduce the damage from recurring fires.Leonardo DiCaprio’s conservation group supports wider effortsThe Pantanal project is part of a broader conservation program backed by Re:wld that works with local organizations, indigenous communities and conservation professionals across Brazil.A conservation-focused trip by a delegation led by senior Brazil representative Rodrigo Medeiros and Re:wild founder Leonardo DiCaprio took them through the Amazon, Pantanal and Cerrado during a recent visit to the country. The group met with government officials, Indigenous leaders, scientists and local conservation groups to discuss how to protect biodiversity, restore wildlife populations and strengthen Indigenous rights.In the Pantanal, the delegation visited Caiman, a conservation lodge and research property, and Fazenda Santa Tereza, part of the Alto Pantanal Corridor. Re highlighted the work of Onçafari and other partners working in the recovery of jaguars and protection of public and private conservation landscapes.It also said it helped efforts to protect some 326,180 acres in the Taquari Wetlands with private reserves and a planned new state park.Connecting Conservation in BrazilRe:wild is involved in much more than the Pantanal. The organization and its Brazilian partners are backing the Southern Amazon Shield, an initiative to protect more than 14 million acres of forests, rivers and other ecosystems on a major deforestation frontier in the southern Amazon.It also does work to support Indigenous-led conservation. The Chief Raoni Legacy Fund, supported by Re and led by Instituto Raoni, will provide long-term financing for the protection of nearly 8,000 square miles of Kayapó Indigenous territory.According to Re:wild, its fire-related investments in Brazil in 2023 and 2024, including from the Bezos Earth Fund, totaled about $8.5 million. These investments helped bolster protection across vulnerable landscapes by supporting firefighter training and equipment, and Indigenous associations and community fire brigades.The expansion of the two Pantanal reserves in March adds yet another important layer to these efforts. The latest conservation action in Brazil offers greater security for wildlife and communities that depend on one of the world’s most remarkable ecosystems by protecting more wetlands, linking habitats and strengthening the landscape against fires.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and istock
